type: classifying — used in practice, not only in theory
position: attributive only — *applied math*; after a verb *applied* is the verb: *The rule was applied*

senses.gloss: Used for practical purposes rather than studied only as theory.
examples: She has a degree in *applied* mathematics.
The lab focuses on *applied* research, not basic science.
*Applied* linguistics looks at real problems like language teaching.

position: attributive only — *an appointed official*, *at the appointed time*; after a verb it is the passive: *She was appointed*
contrast: *well-appointed* is a different idea: a room or hotel that is well furnished and equipped.

senses.gloss: Chosen for a job by someone in authority, not elected.
examples: The *appointed* judge will serve for life.
Most school board members here are elected, not *appointed*.
The mayor's *appointed* adviser resigned after a month.

senses.gloss: Decided or agreed on in advance.
examples: We met at the *appointed* time.
Everyone gathered at the *appointed* place outside the station.

senses.gloss: Large or important enough to be noticed or measured.
examples: There was no *appreciable* difference between the two brands.
The new law had an *appreciable* effect on traffic deaths.
The change in temperature was small but *appreciable*.

senses.gloss: Feeling or showing thanks.
examples: We're very *appreciative* of your help.
She wrote an *appreciative* note to the nurses.
The kids could be a little more *appreciative* of what they have.

senses.gloss: Enjoying something and understanding its value.
examples: The band played to an *appreciative* crowd.
He's an *appreciative* reader of old science fiction.

contrast: It means worried about what may happen, not *understanding*: the verb *apprehend* means *to arrest*, and only rarely *to grasp*.

senses.gloss: Worried or a little afraid that something bad will happen.
examples: I was *apprehensive* about starting a new job.
She gave me an *apprehensive* look.
Voters grew more *apprehensive* as prices kept rising.

senses.gloss: Friendly and easy to talk to.
examples: Our new manager is really *approachable*.
Try to seem more *approachable* at the front desk.
She's the most *approachable* professor in the department.

senses.gloss: Easy to understand or enjoy, even for beginners.
examples: The book makes physics *approachable* for teenagers.
It's an *approachable* wine that goes with almost anything.

contrast: The verb *appropriate* (uh-PROH-pree-ayt) means to take something for yourself, often without permission. The adjective ends in *-uht*.

senses.gloss: Right or suitable for a particular situation.
examples: Jeans aren't *appropriate* for a job interview.
Please take *appropriate* action.
A handshake would have been more *appropriate* than a hug.

senses.gloss: Officially accepted as good enough or allowed.
examples: Use only *approved* chargers with this phone.
Is this car seat *approved* for airplanes?
Pick a book from the *approved* reading list.

senses.gloss: Showing that you think someone or something is good.
examples: Her dad gave an *approving* nod.
The critics were mostly *approving*.
My parents were never very *approving* of my friends.

contrast: The verb *approximate* (uh-PRAHK-suh-mayt) means to come close to. The adjective ends in *-muht*.

senses.gloss: Close to the correct number or amount, but not exact.
examples: What's the *approximate* cost of the repair?
The *approximate* driving time is four hours.
These numbers are only *approximate*.

contrast: Also said uh-KWAH-tik. *Aquatic* is for living things and activities; ordinary *water* covers most other uses: *a water bottle*, not ✗ *an aquatic bottle*.

senses.gloss: Living in water or happening in water.
examples: Frogs and turtles are *aquatic* animals.
The city built a new *aquatic* center with three pools.
Some of these plants are fully *aquatic*.

contrast: *Arabian* is for the Arabian Peninsula and a few fixed names (*an Arabian horse*, *the Arabian Sea*, *Arabian Nights*). For people use *Arab*; for the language use *Arabic*: ✗ *Arabian language* → *Arabic*.

senses.gloss: Related to Arabia, the peninsula between the Red Sea and the Persian Gulf.
examples: The *Arabian* Peninsula is mostly desert.
She rides an *Arabian* horse.
Oman lies on the *Arabian* Sea.

senses.gloss: Good for growing crops.
examples: Only a small part of the country is *arable* land.
The farm has two hundred acres of *arable* fields.
Much of the soil there is too salty to be *arable*.

contrast: Not *арбитражный*. It means based on chance or someone's whim, not on a reason.

senses.gloss: Chosen or done by chance or personal whim, not for a reason.
examples: The age limit seems completely *arbitrary*.
Workers complained about *arbitrary* rules.
The new deadline is even more *arbitrary* than the old one.

senses.gloss: Known or understood by very few people; hard to understand.
examples: The tax code is full of *arcane* rules.
He has an *arcane* knowledge of baseball statistics.
The debate got more *arcane* as the night went on.

contrast: American writing also uses the spelling *archeological*; both are correct in the US.

senses.gloss: Related to archaeology, the study of the past through old objects and buildings.
examples: The site is an important *archaeological* find.
Students joined an *archaeological* dig in New Mexico.
The museum shows *archaeological* evidence of early farming.

senses.gloss: Very old or old-fashioned, and no longer in ordinary use.
examples: The state still has some *archaic* laws on the books.
*Thou* is an *archaic* word for *you*.
Their billing system is even more *archaic* than ours.

senses.gloss: Shaped like an arch, curving up in the middle.
examples: The church has tall *arched* windows.
She raised one *arched* eyebrow.
The cat's back was *arched* and its tail was puffed up.

senses.gloss: Being a perfect, typical example of something.
examples: It's the *archetypal* small Midwestern town.
He was the *archetypal* self-made businessman.
Few stories are more *archetypal* than the hero's journey.

senses.gloss: Related to architecture or the design of buildings.
examples: Chicago is famous for its *architectural* history.
The house has some unusual *architectural* details.
She works at an *architectural* firm downtown.

senses.gloss: Related to or kept in an archive of old records.
examples: The documentary uses a lot of *archival* footage.
Researchers spent weeks in the *archival* collections.
Print the photos on *archival* paper so they don't fade.

contrast: Many Americans drop the first *c*: AHR-tik. In the 'very cold' sense it is often written with a small letter: *arctic air*.

senses.gloss: Related to the area around the North Pole.
examples: Polar bears live on the *Arctic* sea ice.
The *Arctic* Ocean is warming fast.
They joined an *Arctic* research expedition.

senses.gloss: Extremely cold.
examples: An *arctic* blast hit the Midwest this week.
The office air conditioning is *arctic*.

senses.gloss: Showing strong, eager feelings of support or love.
examples: He's an *ardent* supporter of gun control.
She has been an *ardent* Yankees fan since childhood.
Even his most *ardent* admirers were disappointed.

senses.gloss: Very hard and tiring, needing a lot of effort.
examples: It was an *arduous* climb to the top.
Getting a green card can be a long and *arduous* process.
The return trip was even more *arduous*.

contrast: *Argentinian* means the same and is common in the US. The ending is also said -tyn (AHR-juhn-tyn).

senses.gloss: From or related to Argentina.
examples: We had dinner at an *Argentine* steakhouse.
The *Argentine* team won the World Cup.
Her mother is *Argentine* and her father is Canadian.

position: both — mostly after a verb: *It is arguable that…*
contrast: Two opposite-looking uses: *it's arguable that he was right* means you can make a good case that he was right; *whether it worked is arguable* means it is open to doubt. The adverb *arguably* (*arguably the best*) is far more common.

senses.gloss: Possible to support with good reasons.
examples: It's *arguable* that the old system worked better.
She has an *arguable* claim to the land.

senses.gloss: Not certain; open to disagreement.
examples: Whether the plan saved any money is *arguable*.
The referee made an *arguable* call in the last minute.

senses.gloss: Often starting arguments or disagreeing with people.
examples: He gets *argumentative* when he's tired.
She's the most *argumentative* person in the family.

senses.gloss: Presenting reasons to support an opinion.
examples: For homework, write an *argumentative* essay on school uniforms.
The article is more *argumentative* than informative.

senses.gloss: Having very little rain; too dry for many plants.
examples: Much of Arizona has an *arid* climate.
Cactuses grow well in *arid* regions.
The land gets more *arid* the farther west you drive.

senses.gloss: Dull and without life or interest.
examples: The report was long and *arid*.
He found the lectures intellectually *arid*.

comparison: more/most — *more aristocratic*, *most aristocratic*, in the 'manner' sense

senses.gloss: Belonging to the highest social class.
examples: She comes from an old *aristocratic* family.
The novel is set in *aristocratic* circles of 19th-century Russia.

senses.gloss: Looking or behaving like an aristocrat: elegant, proud, or superior.
examples: He had a thin, *aristocratic* face.
Her manners were even more *aristocratic* than her mother's.

senses.gloss: Related to the Greek philosopher Aristotle or his ideas.
examples: The course begins with *Aristotelian* logic.
His argument follows an *Aristotelian* model of ethics.
*Aristotelian* ideas shaped medieval science.

position: both — in the 'involving weapons' sense only before a noun: *armed robbery*

senses.gloss: Carrying a weapon, especially a gun.
examples: Two *armed* men robbed the store.
Police said the suspect was *armed* and dangerous.
Should school guards be *armed*?

senses.gloss: Involving the use of weapons.
examples: He is serving time for *armed* robbery.
The *armed* conflict has lasted ten years.

senses.gloss: Having the tools or knowledge you need.
examples: She came to the meeting *armed* with facts.
We went out *armed* with sunscreen and bug spray.

senses.gloss: From or related to Armenia, its people or its language.
examples: Los Angeles has a large *Armenian* community.
We ordered *Armenian* flatbread.
Her grandparents were *Armenian*.

contrast: American spelling; British English writes *armoured*.

senses.gloss: Covered with armor or a hard protective layer.
examples: An *armored* truck picks up cash from the bank.
The army sent in *armored* vehicles.
Armadillos are *armored* with bony plates.

senses.gloss: Having a strong, pleasant smell.
examples: The kitchen was full of *aromatic* spices.
Fresh basil is very *aromatic*.
Toasting the cumin makes it even more *aromatic*.

position: attributive only — with hyphens before a noun; after a verb it is the adverb phrase *around the clock*, without hyphens
contrast: *The store is open around the clock* is an adverb phrase. Only before a noun (*around-the-clock care*) is it an adjective. British English prefers *round-the-clock*.

senses.gloss: Happening all day and all night without stopping.
examples: My grandmother needs *around-the-clock* care.
The hospital has *around-the-clock* security.
Crews did *around-the-clock* repairs after the storm.

contrast: *Aroused* as an adjective usually means sexually excited, so be careful with it. For interest or suspicion use the verb: *The noise aroused his suspicion*.

senses.gloss: Sexually excited.
examples: The article explains what happens in the body when people feel *aroused*.
Some medications make it harder to become *aroused*.

senses.gloss: Stirred up to strong feeling or action.
examples: An *aroused* public demanded answers.
The dog was fully *aroused* and barking at the door.

position: attributive only — *an arranged marriage*; after a verb it is the passive: *The meeting was arranged*

senses.gloss: Planned in advance by other people, especially a marriage chosen by the families.
examples: Her parents had an *arranged* marriage.
*Arranged* marriages are still common in some countries.
The two leaders met at an *arranged* location.

contrast: *An arresting image* has nothing to do with the police; it grabs your attention. *The arresting officer* is different: the officer who made the arrest, before a noun only.

senses.gloss: So striking that it catches your attention.
examples: She has *arresting* green eyes.
The magazine cover was bold and *arresting*.
It's one of the most *arresting* photos of the war.

senses.gloss: Acting as if you are better or more important than other people.
examples: He's smart but incredibly *arrogant*.
I didn't like her *arrogant* tone.
Success made him even more *arrogant*.

contrast: Not the same as *artistic*. *Artful* is about skill, and sometimes about clever tricks.

senses.gloss: Done with skill and cleverness.
examples: The film is an *artful* mix of comedy and drama.
The chef's plates were small and *artful*.

senses.gloss: Clever at getting what you want, often by tricking people.
examples: He gave an *artful* answer that avoided the question.
She was the most *artful* negotiator in the room.

senses.gloss: Having arthritis, a disease that makes joints painful and stiff.
examples: Our old dog has *arthritic* hips.
Her hands are too *arthritic* to open jars.
His knees got more *arthritic* every winter.

senses.gloss: Related to the stories of King Arthur and his knights.
senses.ru: артуровский, связанный с легендами о короле Артуре
examples: She teaches a class on *Arthurian* legends.
Merlin is a famous *Arthurian* character.
The movie is a loose retelling of an *Arthurian* tale.

contrast: The verb *articulate* (ahr-TIK-yuh-layt) means to express or pronounce clearly. The adjective ends in *-luht*.

senses.gloss: Able to express ideas clearly and well.
examples: She's a smart, *articulate* speaker.
He's much more *articulate* in writing than in person.

senses.gloss: Expressed clearly and easy to understand.
examples: The lawyer gave an *articulate* argument.
It was the most *articulate* explanation of the problem I've heard.

comparison: more/most — *more artificial*, *most artificial*, in the 'not sincere' sense; not gradable in the 'man-made' sense

senses.gloss: Made by people, often as a copy of something natural.
examples: The drink has no *artificial* colors.
We put up an *artificial* Christmas tree this year.
*Artificial* intelligence is changing a lot of jobs.

senses.gloss: Not sincere or natural in behavior.
examples: She gave me a big, *artificial* smile.
The conversation felt stiff and *artificial*, even more *artificial* than the last one.

contrast: Today the word is tied to Nazi and white-supremacist ideas about a 'pure' white race, so it appears mostly in history books and news about hate groups. Scholars now say *Indo-Iranian* or *Indo-European* for the old linguistic sense.

senses.gloss: In Nazi and white-supremacist ideology, belonging to a supposed superior white race.
examples: The Nazis promoted a false myth of an *Aryan* master race.
The prison gang calls itself an *Aryan* brotherhood.
Historians explain how the idea of *Aryan* superiority was invented.

contrast: *In the ascendant* uses the noun and means the same: *Her career is in the ascendant*. Sometimes spelled *ascendent*.

senses.gloss: Becoming more powerful or influential.
examples: The party's younger wing is now *ascendant*.
Streaming is the *ascendant* force in entertainment.
By the 1980s, the conservative movement was *ascendant*.

senses.gloss: Going up, or arranged from the lowest or smallest to the highest or largest.
examples: List the numbers in *ascending* order.
Sort the prices from low to high, in *ascending* order.
The song ends on an *ascending* scale.

contrast: Do not confuse with *aesthetic* (es-THET-ik), which is about beauty. *An ascetic* is also a noun: a person who lives this way.

senses.gloss: Living a very simple life without comfort or pleasure, often for religious reasons.
examples: The monks lead an *ascetic* life.
His apartment was clean and almost *ascetic*.
She became more *ascetic* as she got older.

senses.gloss: In biology, happening without two parents or sex cells.
examples: Some starfish use *asexual* reproduction.
Many plants can reproduce in an *asexual* way.

senses.gloss: Not feeling sexual attraction to other people.
examples: He came out as *asexual* in college.
The show has an *asexual* main character.

senses.gloss: Very pale gray, especially of a face, from shock, fear or illness.
examples: His face went *ashen* when he heard the news.
She walked out of the doctor's office looking *ashen*.
The *ashen* sky warned of more smoke from the fires.

contrast: From Latin *asinus*, 'donkey'. It is strong and insulting.

senses.gloss: Extremely stupid or silly.
examples: That's the most *asinine* rule I've ever heard.
He made an *asinine* comment about her weight.
The whole argument was *asinine*.

position: predicative only — also after an object: *The wind knocked his hat askew*
contrast: Russian uses an adverb (*криво*, *набок*); English uses *askew* after *be* or after an object, never before a noun: ✗ *an askew picture* → *a crooked picture*.

senses.gloss: Not straight or not in the right position.
examples: His tie was *askew*.
The picture on the wall hung slightly *askew*.
She came in with her glasses *askew*.

senses.gloss: Hoping and working to become a particular kind of person.
examples: She's an *aspiring* actress in Los Angeles.
The workshop is for *aspiring* writers.
*Aspiring* doctors have to study for years.

contrast: In American English *assertive* is usually a compliment: confident and clear, not rude. *Aggressive* is the negative word.

senses.gloss: Confident and direct in saying what you want or think.
examples: You need to be more *assertive* in meetings.
She took an *assertive* approach to the negotiations.
He's quiet, but he can be *assertive* when it matters.

senses.gloss: Working very carefully and with steady effort.
examples: She's an *assiduous* student who never misses class.
Thanks to *assiduous* research, the reporter found the documents.
He was the most *assiduous* note-taker in the room.

senses.gloss: Given to a particular person as their place, share or task.
examples: Please go to your *assigned* seats.
Did you finish the *assigned* reading?
Parking at our office is *assigned*, so don't take someone else's spot.

contrast: As a noun (*my assistant*) it is a person. Before a job title it means second in rank: *assistant manager* is *заместитель управляющего*. In US universities an *assistant professor* is a junior professor, below *associate professor*.

senses.gloss: Helping and working under the person in charge.
examples: He works as an *assistant* manager at a grocery store.
The *assistant* coach took over after the head coach quit.
She was hired as an *assistant* professor of history.

contrast: *Assisted living* is a US term for housing where older people get help with daily tasks but do not need a nursing home.

senses.gloss: Done or provided with help from another person or a machine.
examples: My grandfather moved into an *assisted* living facility.
The car has power-*assisted* steering.
The clinic offers *assisted* reproduction for couples.

senses.gloss: Designed to help people with disabilities do things.
examples: Screen readers are a kind of *assistive* technology.
The school provides *assistive* devices for students who need them.
Hearing aids are the most common *assistive* device.

contrast: The verb *associate* (uh-SOH-see-ayt) means to connect in the mind. In US universities an *associate professor* ranks above an *assistant professor*; an *associate degree* is a two-year college degree. Also said uh-SOH-shee-uht.

senses.gloss: Having a position just below the top rank, or less than full membership.
examples: She was promoted to *associate* professor.
He's an *associate* editor at the magazine.
He got an *associate* degree from a community college.

senses.gloss: Of several different kinds mixed together.
examples: She brought a box of *assorted* chocolates.
The T-shirts come in *assorted* colors.
The cookies in the tin are *assorted*.

senses.gloss: False and used to hide who you are.
examples: He lived for years under an *assumed* name.
She checked into the hotel under an *assumed* identity.

senses.gloss: Believed to be true without proof.
examples: The *assumed* cause of the fire was a faulty heater.
The plan depends on an *assumed* growth rate of three percent.

comparison: more/most — *more assured*, *most assured*, in the 'confident' sense
contrast: *Rest assured* is a fixed phrase: *Rest assured, we'll fix it* means *будьте уверены*.

senses.gloss: Confident and calm.
examples: She gave an *assured* performance in her first big role.
He seemed more *assured* after a few weeks on the job.

senses.gloss: Certain to happen or to be received.
examples: With this win, the team's place in the playoffs is *assured*.
Members are *assured* of a seat at every show.

contrast: The *th* in *asthma* and *asthmatic* is silent.

senses.gloss: Having asthma, or caused by asthma.
examples: Their son is *asthmatic*, so they can't have a cat.
Smoke is dangerous for *asthmatic* children.
I heard an *asthmatic* wheeze from the back seat.

contrast: *Astounded* is how you feel; *astounding* is what causes the feeling.

senses.gloss: Very surprised or shocked.
examples: I was *astounded* at how much the tickets cost.
We were *astounded* to hear she had quit.
The *astounded* crowd went silent.

senses.gloss: So surprising that it is hard to believe.
examples: The show was an *astounding* success.
The amount of food they wasted was *astounding*.
It's the most *astounding* comeback in the history of the sport.

senses.gloss: Related to astrology, the belief that stars and planets affect people's lives.
examples: What's your *astrological* sign?
She reads her *astrological* forecast every morning.
The app gives *astrological* advice about dating.

position: both — in the 'science' sense only before a noun
comparison: not gradable — in the 'huge' sense it is extreme: *absolutely astronomical*, *truly astronomical*

senses.gloss: Extremely large, especially of prices or amounts.
examples: Rents in San Francisco are *astronomical*.
The hospital sent us an *astronomical* bill.
The odds of winning are *astronomical*.

senses.gloss: Related to astronomy, the study of stars and planets.
examples: The observatory has an *astronomical* telescope open to the public.
*Astronomical* data showed a new planet.

senses.gloss: Quick to notice and understand things, and to use this to your advantage.
examples: She's an *astute* businesswoman.
That's a very *astute* observation.
He was more *astute* than his rivals about what voters wanted.

contrast: Same meaning as *asymmetrical*, but *asymmetric* is the usual form in technical phrases: *asymmetric warfare*, *asymmetric information*.

senses.gloss: Having two sides or halves that are not the same.
examples: The building has an *asymmetric* roof.
Her face is slightly *asymmetric*, like most people's.

senses.gloss: Unequal in power, size or information between two sides.
examples: It was an *asymmetric* war between an army and small rebel groups.
Sellers often have *asymmetric* information about a used car.

senses.gloss: Having two sides or halves that are different in shape or size.
examples: She got an *asymmetrical* haircut.
The dress has an *asymmetrical* hem.
The second design is even more *asymmetrical*.

senses.gloss: Having an illness but showing no signs of it.
examples: Many people with the virus are *asymptomatic*.
*Asymptomatic* carriers can still infect others.
The test found an *asymptomatic* infection.

senses.gloss: Not happening at the same time; letting people take part at different times.
examples: The online course is *asynchronous*, so you can watch lectures anytime.
Email is an *asynchronous* way to communicate.
The app uses *asynchronous* updates to save battery.

takes: *for* + noun (*at a loss for words*); *to*-infinitive; *as to* + wh-clause
contrast: *Sell at a loss* (себе в убыток) is a different, adverbial use about money.

senses.gloss: Not knowing what to do, say or think.
examples: For once, she was *at a loss* for words.
I'm completely *at a loss* as to why he left.
Doctors were *at a loss* to explain her symptoms.

contrast: Not *в ошибке*: it means responsible for something bad. *An at-fault driver* is a US insurance term, with hyphens before a noun.

senses.gloss: Responsible for a mistake, accident or problem.
examples: The other driver was *at fault* for the accident.
Nobody wants to admit they're *at fault*.
Who was more *at fault*, the company or the city?

position: after the noun — *the task at hand*; also predicative: *Help is at hand*

senses.gloss: Being dealt with now.
examples: Let's focus on the problem *at hand*.
He had trouble staying on the topic *at hand*.

senses.gloss: Close by and easy to reach.
examples: Keep a flashlight close *at hand* during storms.
Always have your ID *at hand* at the airport.

senses.gloss: About to happen soon.
examples: Summer vacation is *at hand*.
The protesters said a new era was *at hand*.

position: after the noun — *the public at large*; also predicative: *The suspect is at large*; before a noun as *at-large*
contrast: In US politics *at-large* (with a hyphen, before a noun) means elected by the whole city or state, not by one district: *an at-large council seat*.

senses.gloss: Free and not yet caught.
examples: The escaped prisoner is still *at large*.
Police warned that the gunman remained *at large*.

senses.gloss: As a whole; in general.
examples: The new rules affect society *at large*.
The public *at large* knows little about the program.

senses.gloss: Representing a whole area rather than one district.
senses.ru: избираемый от всего округа, города или штата
examples: She won an *at-large* seat on the city council.
Wyoming has only one *at-large* representative in Congress.

senses.gloss: Strongly disagreeing and unable to settle an argument.
senses.ru: в конфликте, в ссоре, на ножах
examples: The union and management are *at loggerheads* over pay.
He's been *at loggerheads* with his neighbor for years.
The two parties remain *at loggerheads* on the budget.

senses.gloss: Disagreeing with someone.
examples: The mayor is *at odds* with the city council.
The brothers have been *at odds* over the family business.

senses.gloss: Not matching; in conflict with something.
examples: His story is *at odds* with the video evidence.
Her quiet voice seemed *at odds* with her tough reputation.

comparison: more/most — *more at peace*, *most at peace*, in the 'calm' sense

senses.gloss: Calm and content, without worry.
examples: I finally feel *at peace* with my decision.
She seemed more *at peace* after she moved to the country.

senses.gloss: Not at war.
examples: The two countries have been *at peace* for decades.
The region was *at peace* for the first time in years.

senses.gloss: Dead, used gently to comfort people.
examples: After a long illness, Grandpa is *at peace* now.
We take comfort knowing she's *at peace*.

position: predicative only — also after a noun: *phones at the ready*

senses.gloss: Prepared and available to be used right away.
examples: Reporters waited with cameras *at the ready*.
Keep a fire extinguisher *at the ready* in the kitchen.
The nurses were *at the ready* when the ambulance arrived.

type: origin — religion or lack of it
contrast: Mostly a noun (*She's an atheist*), but Americans also say *she's atheist* and *an atheist group*. *Atheistic* is the more formal adjective.

senses.gloss: Not believing that God or gods exist.
examples: He grew up in an *atheist* household.
She's *atheist*, but she still loves Christmas.
The *atheist* club meets on campus every Thursday.

senses.gloss: From or related to Athens, especially ancient Athens.
examples: We studied *Athenian* democracy in history class.
Socrates was an *Athenian* philosopher.
The ship was *Athenian*, not Spartan.

position: both — in the 'sports' sense only before a noun
comparison: more/most — *more athletic*, *most athletic*, in the 'fit' sense
contrast: Three syllables: ath-LET-ik, not ✗ ath-uh-LET-ik. In the US *athletic* covers all sports (*athletic shoes*, *the athletic department*); British *athletics* means only track and field.

senses.gloss: Physically strong, fit and good at sports.
examples: She's tall and very *athletic*.
He's more *athletic* than his brother.
The job requires an *athletic* build.

senses.gloss: Related to sports and physical exercise.
examples: He got an *athletic* scholarship to play football.
I need new *athletic* shoes.

senses.gloss: Related to the Atlantic Ocean or the lands along it.
examples: They live on the *Atlantic* coast of Florida.
The *Atlantic* hurricane season starts in June.
Maryland is one of the Mid-*Atlantic* states.

position: both — in the 'air' sense only before a noun
comparison: more/most — *more atmospheric*, *most atmospheric*, in the 'mood' sense
contrast: Also said at-muh-SFER-ik.

senses.gloss: Related to the air around the earth.
examples: *Atmospheric* pressure drops before a storm.
Scientists measure *atmospheric* carbon dioxide levels.

senses.gloss: Creating a special mood or feeling, often mysterious or romantic.
examples: The restaurant is dark and *atmospheric*.
It's one of the most *atmospheric* horror movies I've seen.

contrast: For weapons and power plants, modern American English usually says *nuclear*; *atomic* sounds historical (*the atomic bomb*, *the Atomic Age*).

senses.gloss: Related to atoms.
examples: Carbon's *atomic* number is six.
The class covered *atomic* structure.

senses.gloss: Related to energy or weapons made by splitting atoms.
examples: The US dropped two *atomic* bombs on Japan in 1945.
The 1950s were called the *Atomic* Age.

senses.gloss: Very bad or unpleasant.
examples: The service at that hotel was *atrocious*.
My handwriting is *atrocious*.
That was the most *atrocious* call a referee has ever made.

senses.gloss: Extremely cruel and shocking.
examples: The soldiers committed *atrocious* crimes.
The prisoners lived in *atrocious* conditions.

position: both — in the 'fond' sense only after a verb
comparison: more/most — *more attached*, *most attached*, in the 'fond' sense; not gradable in the 'joined' sense

senses.gloss: Loving someone or something and not wanting to lose them.
examples: The kids are very *attached* to their grandmother.
I got more *attached* to that old car than I expected.
Don't get too *attached* — it's just a rental.

senses.gloss: Joined or fastened to something.
examples: The house has an *attached* garage.
Please sign the *attached* form and send it back.

senses.gloss: Already in a romantic relationship.
examples: Is your cousin *attached*, or is he single?
All the nice guys I meet are already *attached*.

senses.gloss: Possible to reach or achieve.
examples: Set small, *attainable* goals.
Home ownership no longer feels *attainable* for many young people.
Lower prices made the dream more *attainable*.

contrast: Russian often uses a noun: *attempted murder* is *покушение на убийство*, *an attempted coup* is *попытка переворота*.

senses.gloss: Tried but not successfully completed, especially a crime.
examples: He was charged with *attempted* murder.
Guards stopped an *attempted* escape from the prison.
The *attempted* coup failed within hours.

position: both — before a noun (*the attendant risks*) or after a noun with *on* or *upon*
contrast: Much more common as a noun: *a flight attendant*, *a parking attendant*. The adjective is formal.

senses.gloss: Happening together with or as a result of something.
examples: Fame brought all its *attendant* problems.
The move to a big city had its *attendant* costs.
The dangers *attendant* on the job are well known.

senses.gloss: Designed to make people notice.
examples: The ad uses bright, *attention-getting* colors.
He opened his speech with an *attention-getting* story.
Her second headline was even more *attention-getting*.

senses.gloss: Listening or watching carefully.
examples: The students were quiet and *attentive*.
Be more *attentive* to the details.

senses.gloss: Taking care of someone's needs; thoughtful.
examples: The waiter was friendly and *attentive*.
He's always been an *attentive* husband.

senses.gloss: Pleasant to look at, especially in a sexual or romantic way.
examples: She's a very *attractive* woman.
He found her smile *attractive*.
The town is more *attractive* in the fall.

senses.gloss: Having qualities that make you want it.
examples: They made me an *attractive* job offer.
Low interest rates make buying a home more *attractive*.

position: predicative only — or right after a noun: *deaths attributable to smoking*

senses.gloss: Caused by or explained by something.
examples: Most of the delays were *attributable* to the weather.
About twenty percent of the cases are *attributable* to diet.
Deaths *attributable* to heat have gone up.

senses.gloss: Not typical or usual.
examples: This warm weather is *atypical* for January.
The patient had *atypical* symptoms.
That kind of anger is *atypical* of him.

position: after the noun — *potatoes au gratin*; also before it: *au gratin potatoes*
contrast: Also said oh GRAT-uhn. In American menus it almost always means baked with cheese on top.

senses.gloss: Covered with cheese or breadcrumbs and baked until brown.
examples: We had ham and potatoes *au gratin* for Easter.
I made an *au gratin* dish with cauliflower.
The broccoli *au gratin* was the best part of the meal.

position: after the noun — *prime rib au jus*
contrast: On US menus people often treat it as a noun (*a French dip with au jus*), and many say oh JOOS; strictly it means 'served with its juice'.

senses.gloss: Served with the juices that came out of the meat while cooking.
senses.ru: в собственном соку, с мясным соусом
examples: He ordered the prime rib *au jus*.
The roast beef sandwich comes *au jus*.
Serve the beef *au jus* with mashed potatoes.

contrast: Used almost only for hair. Not the same as Russian *рыжий* (that is *red* or *ginger*): *auburn* is a darker reddish brown.

senses.gloss: Reddish brown, especially of hair.
examples: She has long *auburn* hair.
His beard was a darker *auburn* than his hair.
Her curls looked almost *auburn* in the sunlight.
